intro: Read the deck for the method and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you a way to remember it and warns where people slip. Work the section exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions before you look, and run the checks on a draft map of your own.

sections.title: What a Theory of Change Is
sections.big_idea: A theory of change is an **explicit, testable causal map** from activities to long-term change, with the assumptions named.
in_plain_words: Four demands define it: it must be explicit, causal, testable and assumption-bearing. The shape runs from activities through outputs and outcomes to impact, and each arrow is a claim. A plan, a workplan, a logframe filled in afterwards or a diagram drawn to please a donor can look like a ToC and do none of its work.

The idea grew out of Carol Weiss's 1995 argument that unstated theories made initiatives impossible to evaluate. It then became a design tool, and donors made it a requirement. Use a diagram for structure and a narrative for reasoning, anchor both in a context, and expect the team to disagree while drafting.

right.title: Otherwise it is
items: A list of things you will do

key_terms.meaning: An explicit, testable account of how and why activities lead to long-term change.
Some observation from monitoring could contradict it.
A linear line of boxes with no stated because on the arrows.
The written story that explains each pathway, assumptions and evidence.
The place, people, politics and services the theory assumes.

worked_example.title: Diagnose four documents
worked_example.setup: Four documents each claim to be a ToC. Use the symptom table on slide 6 to say what each really is.
steps: Every box is a verb such as train, build or convene: a workplan.
The arrows carry no because: a results chain.
It was written after the design to defend it: a justification.
It has only one pathway: a results chain again.
Weiss wrote in 1995 and Vogel reviewed practice in 2012: 2012 − 1995 = 17 years of ToC use in development.
worked_example.answer: A workplan, two results chains and a justification. None is a ToC until it carries a testable because, a second pathway and a link to monitoring.

mistakes: Treating the diagram as the whole ToC. Without the narrative the reasoning is lost within a staffing cycle.
Accepting a ToC nobody argued over. It has not surfaced the team's differing theories.
Leaving the context unstated. The same activity can have different outcomes in different settings.

recall.q: What four things must a ToC be?
recall.a: Explicit, causal, testable and assumption-bearing.

recall.q: What did Carol Weiss argue in 1995?
recall.a: Complex initiatives failed evaluation because their theories were left unstated and untested.

recall.q: What practical test shows a map is more than decoration?
recall.a: You can name one monitoring finding that would make you redraw it.

recall.q: Which row of the context table do design teams skip?
recall.a: Other actors: whether you are the binding constraint.

recall.q: How long should the diagram and narrative be?
recall.a: One page for the diagram and two to five pages for the narrative.

sections.title: Why ToC Matters
sections.big_idea: A ToC does four jobs for you, **but only if the team builds it and its assumptions are monitored**.
in_plain_words: The four jobs are shared understanding, better design, sharper evaluation and faster learning. Each is conditional on process: the team must build it, draw it before the design is fixed, take indicators from the map and monitor the assumptions. A ToC shifts effort up the chain toward outcomes.

A ToC differs from a plan because it asks how and why, works backwards from the goal and says what would disprove it. It surfaces differing theories while they are cheap to resolve, exposes missing links, supplies evaluation questions and keeps claims honest through three spheres: control, influence and interest.

key_terms.meaning: Activities and outputs you own.
Outcomes you contribute to.
Impact shaped by many actors.
Evaluation that tests each link of the ToC.
Evidence that would show the theory is wrong.

worked_example.title: Which sphere does each claim sit in?
worked_example.setup: Apply the claim language from slide 20 to four statements about a teacher-training programme.
steps: '200 teachers trained' sits in control: we delivered it, shown by programme records.
'Teachers use the method' sits in influence: we contributed to it, shown by comparison or contribution analysis.
'More children read at grade level' sits in interest: many actors shape it, so it sits within context data.
Which spheres carry a target? Control and influence can; the impact row carries none.
worked_example.answer: Control, influence and interest in that order. The claim language is 'we delivered', 'we contributed to' and 'this sits within'.

mistakes: Commissioning a ToC from a consultant at the end. It delivers none of the four jobs.
Writing an impact-level sentence in a proposal. Three years later it becomes the standard you are judged against.
Treating a ToC and a plan as rivals. A programme needs both: the failure is substituting one for the other.

recall.q: Name the four jobs of a ToC.
recall.a: Shared understanding, better design, sharper evaluation and faster learning.

recall.q: What does a plan ask and what does a ToC ask?
recall.a: A plan asks what we will do by when. A ToC asks how and why change happens.

recall.q: What does a ToC tell the evaluator?
recall.a: What to measure, which arrows to test and which assumptions to question.

recall.q: Which three spheres come from Outcome Mapping?
recall.a: Control, influence and interest.

recall.q: When is resolving differing theories cheapest?
recall.a: At design, in a workshop, against a redesign in year two or a failed evaluation.

sections.title: ToC vs Logframe vs Results Chain
sections.big_idea: The three tools **nest**. Build the ToC first, draw the chain out of it, and summarise it as a logframe.
in_plain_words: A results chain is the linear spine, a logframe is a four-by-four matrix for management and M&E, and a ToC adds branching pathways, assumptions on every arrow, a rationale and a narrative. Each loses something: the chain loses why, the logframe loses the reasoning between rows, and the ToC loses compactness.

A filled-in logframe does not prove a ToC. Test it with four questions about why, what must hold, what evidence supports the link and what else could produce the outcome. Deriving a ToC from a finished logframe is reverse-engineering. Related methods such as contribution analysis pair well with a ToC.

levels.label: Theory of change
levels.sub: the full causal model and assumptions

levels.label: Results chain
levels.sub: the linear spine drawn out of it

diagram.caption: top first: each layer is derived from the one above

key_terms.meaning: A 4×4 matrix of levels and columns for management and M&E.
Where the evidence for an indicator comes from.
Building a ToC from a finished plan so that it justifies the plan.
Testing the pathway where no control group exists.
Finding outcomes retrospectively in unpredictable settings.

worked_example.title: The assumption cells that do not fit
worked_example.setup: A team has a ToC map with 15 arrows and must hand its funder a logframe.
steps: A logframe has 4 levels and 4 columns: 4 × 4 = 16 cells.
Only one column holds assumptions, so it has 4 assumption cells.
The map has 15 arrows and so 15 assumptions: 15 − 4 = 11 assumptions have no cell.
Put the 11 in the narrative and the monitoring plan, and keep the matrix as a summary.
worked_example.answer: The matrix has 16 cells, 4 of them for assumptions, so 11 of the map's 15 assumptions need another home.

mistakes: Saying 'we have a logframe, so we have a ToC'. A matrix can be complete while the because is unstated.
Producing the three documents independently. They disagree, and it surfaces at evaluation.
Handing over a logframe when a ToC was asked for, without saying what the document does not contain.

recall.q: How many levels and columns does a logframe have?
recall.a: Four levels and four columns.

recall.q: Which order should you build the three tools in?
recall.a: ToC first, then results chain, then logframe.

recall.q: What is the sharpest contrast in the assumption column?
recall.a: A logframe has one per level and a ToC has one per arrow.

recall.q: Name two of the four questions to ask of a logframe.
recall.a: Why does this output produce this outcome, what must hold, what evidence supports the link, what else could produce this outcome.

recall.q: When would you reach for Outcome Harvesting?
recall.a: In unpredictable environments, where outcomes are found retrospectively.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.big_idea: Only the first two links of the chain are yours. **Outcomes and impact are claims about how other people respond.**
in_plain_words: The chain runs inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. Inputs are easy to count and tell a funder little. Outputs are countable products you control. Outcomes are changes in the knowledge, attitudes, behaviour, condition or status of others, and impact is long-term, population-level change shared with many actors.

Calling an output an outcome is the commonest ToC error. Test each box with grammar: if the subject is your own team, it is not an outcome. Outcomes form a ladder from knowledge to behaviour to condition, and the long-term rung is rarely measured. Honest ToCs speak of contribution at impact level.

key_terms.meaning: Financial, human and material resources a programme uses.
Direct, countable product that you control, such as teachers trained.
A change in others: knowledge, attitude, behaviour, condition or status.
Durable, long-term change that many actors shape.
Short-term knowledge, then behaviour, then long-term condition.

worked_example.title: Run the output-or-outcome drill
worked_example.setup: Classify five statements with the test 'did you do it, or did someone else change because of what you did?'. Then size the reclassification on a 20-box map.
steps: '300 farmers attend a seed training' describes what you did: output.
'Farmers sow the improved seed' is someone else's behaviour: outcome.
'District food insecurity falls' is population-level: impact.
'Women attend meetings and speak up' contains 'and': two results to separate.
A quarter of boxes are usually reclassified: 20 × 0.25 = 5 boxes.
worked_example.answer: Output, outcome, impact, two results, and about five boxes of a 20-box map reclassified, almost always downward.

mistakes: Treating spending or burn rate as progress. They are available monthly but are not results.
Stopping at knowledge and attitude outcomes. Behaviour change is a further link, so put it in the map.
Promising a number for impact. Use a national survey series and speak of contribution.

recall.q: Which link of the chain carries most risk and least evidence?
recall.a: Outputs to outcomes.

recall.q: What is the commonest ToC error?
recall.a: Calling an output an outcome.

recall.q: What is the grammar test for an outcome?
recall.a: Someone else does something differently; the subject is not your own team.

recall.q: Why is the long-term outcome rarely measured?
recall.a: The follow-up round has no budget once the project closes.

recall.q: What should accompany each output?
recall.a: One quality indicator, to tell 'delivered' from 'delivered well enough to work'.

sections.title: Backwards Mapping
sections.big_idea: Start from the long-term goal and ask **'what has to be in place first?'** until you reach something you can act on.
in_plain_words: The method comes from ActKnowledge and the Aspen Roundtable. Mapping forwards from activities guarantees the map finds your activities sufficient, while mapping back from the goal shows what the goal requires and exposes gaps as missing boxes. At each step record the precondition, the assumption, the rationale and the actor.

Pathways branch and converge, so map each separately and say whether they are requirements or alternatives. Stop where your reach ends, then ask whether the preconditions are necessary and sufficient. Run it as a workshop with cards on a wall, and protect the final step of surfacing assumptions.

key_terms.meaning: Starting at the long-term goal and asking what must be true just before.
An outcome that must exist before a higher outcome is possible.
The lowest outcome your activities can plausibly act on.
Drop it and the chain breaks.
With all of them true, the next box follows.

worked_example.title: Map back from a goal
worked_example.setup: Illustrative goal: adolescent girls in a block stay in school. Work backwards with the five facilitation steps.
steps: Goal: girls stay enrolled to the end of secondary school.
What must be true just before? They attend regularly, and their families support them.
Repeat: families support them if the costs are manageable and the school is trusted.
Entry point: a family outreach and transport-support activity.
Suppose the goal needs four preconditions and the programme can act on two: 4 − 2 = 2 are out of reach, which is 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5, half.
worked_example.answer: The pathway runs from outreach to support, attendance and enrolment. Half the preconditions sit outside the programme, so partner, advocate or redefine the goal.

mistakes: Starting from the activity list, which guarantees the map confirms what you already do.
Reading convergent pathways as alternatives when they are requirements.
Cutting the assumptions step when the workshop overruns. It is what makes the map testable.

recall.q: Which two bodies are credited with backwards mapping?
recall.a: ActKnowledge and the Aspen Roundtable.

recall.q: What five items do you record at each backward step?
recall.a: The precondition, the assumption, the rationale, the actor, and whether it is an entry point.

recall.q: How do you test sufficiency?
recall.a: Assume all the preconditions are true and check whether the next box follows.

recall.q: What should you do when a necessary entry point is out of reach?
recall.a: Partner, advocate or redefine the goal.

recall.q: Where do you stop mapping?
recall.a: At outcomes your programme can plausibly act on.

sections.title: Assumptions & Rationale
sections.big_idea: Assumptions are **the 'because' in the arrows**, and they are where risk and learning live.
in_plain_words: Every arrow hides a belief about why one outcome leads to the next. There are four kinds: causal-link, rationale or evidence, external condition and diagnostic. The diagnostic one asks whether you identified the binding constraint correctly. Grade the rationale from systematic reviews down to 'it seems reasonable'.

Write each as an IF-THEN-BECAUSE sentence, then plot likelihood against consequence. The same table works as a risk register. Hunt for the load-bearing assumption deliberately, name the external conditions you must watch, and treat each assumption as a hypothesis with a cheap early test.

children.label: Causal-link
items: Why one step leads to the next

children.label: Rationale or evidence
items: Why we believe the link at all

children.label: Diagnostic
items: Did we find the binding constraint?

key_terms.meaning: A condition or belief that must hold for one step to lead to the next.
Evidence, theory or experience that a link tends to hold.
If it fails, the whole theory collapses.
A factor outside your control that you must still name and monitor.
The factor that actually limits change in this setting.

worked_example.title: Audit the arrows and sort the risks
worked_example.setup: Illustrative map with 12 arrows, 5 of which have no stated because. Then place two assumptions on the likelihood and consequence table.
steps: Arrows with a because: 12 − 5 = 7.
Share of silent arrows: 5 ÷ 12 = 0.42, about 42 percent.
'Schools stay open' has low likelihood of failing and high consequence: monitor and keep a contingency.
'Households let women keep earnings' has high likelihood of failing and high consequence: redesign, or do not proceed.
worked_example.answer: Seven arrows are documented and 42 percent are silent. One assumption needs a contingency and one needs a redesign.

mistakes: Accepting 'it is obvious' as a rationale. It carries no weight.
Omitting the diagnostic assumption. A sound chain attached to the wrong problem still fails.
Treating external conditions as an excuse. You can monitor them and adapt.

recall.q: What are the four kinds of assumption?
recall.a: Causal-link, rationale or evidence, external condition and diagnostic.

recall.q: What sentence form surfaces an assumption?
recall.a: IF this, THEN that, BECAUSE of the assumption.

recall.q: How do you test a causal-link assumption?
recall.a: Monitor the two outcomes it connects.

recall.q: What does the top-right corner of the risk plot hold?
recall.a: High likelihood and high consequence: the load-bearing assumptions.

recall.q: What is the most valuable cheap test?
recall.a: Ask non-users why they did not take up the service.

sections.title: Indicators & Evidence
sections.big_idea: A good indicator **moves only if the outcome is real**. Choose few, set baselines first, and name where the data comes from.
in_plain_words: Every outcome needs an indicator. SMART is a useful checklist but it passes a precise measure of something adjacent, so ask what the indicator would read if the programme failed entirely. Match the indicator to the level: counts for outputs, observed practice for medium outcomes, survey or national series for impact.

Use numbers to detect change and stories to understand it. An indicator needs a baseline, a target and a date. Name the means of verification and beware courtesy bias. Attach three indicators to every box and you pay recurring costs for numbers nobody uses.

diagram.note: set the target after the baseline lands, and give the baseline a date and an owner

key_terms.meaning: A measurable marker of whether, and how far, an outcome has happened.
The starting value, measured before you act.
The value you aim for by a stated date.
The data source and method for an indicator.
Reporting more benefit to those who gave you something.

worked_example.title: Judge a result against baseline and target
worked_example.setup: Illustrative outcome indicator: the share of teachers using the new method in class. Baseline 30%, target 45%, endline 41%.
steps: Planned change: 45 − 30 = 15 points.
Achieved change: 41 − 30 = 11 points.
Share of the planned change achieved: 11 ÷ 15 = 0.73, about 73 percent.
Failure check: what would the indicator read if the programme failed entirely? If the answer is still about 30, the indicator can detect change.
worked_example.answer: Teachers using the method rose 11 of a planned 15 points, about 73 percent of the target, and the indicator passes the failure check.

mistakes: Hanging only output indicators on outcome rows. Counting activities says nothing about change.
Writing baselines as 'to be determined'. They overwhelmingly stay undetermined.
Collecting qualitative material after the quantitative result is known, so stories merely illustrate it.

recall.q: What does a good indicator do?
recall.a: It moves only if the outcome is real.

recall.q: What does the S in SMART stand for and test?
recall.a: Specific: would two people measure it the same way?

recall.q: Why must a target come after the baseline?
recall.a: A target set without the starting point is a number and no commitment.

recall.q: What is courtesy bias?
recall.a: People reporting more benefit to the organisation that gave them something than to a neutral enumerator.

recall.q: What question should you ask before adding an indicator?
recall.a: What decision would it change?

sections.title: Drawing the ToC
sections.big_idea: Boxes are changes, arrows are causal claims, and **a map you cannot trace in a minute is too crowded**.
in_plain_words: Each box holds one outcome phrased as a change that has happened, each arrow holds one causal claim with an assumption, and the map reads upward from entry points to the goal. Keep same-level boxes at the same height and number them. Test each box by asking whether you could photograph the change.

Write the narrative beside the map and build both with stakeholders, using cards on a wall. Include the people the change is for, ask who benefits from the status quo, and treat the first draft as a draft. Date every version and push detail into the narrative and indicator table.

key_terms.meaning: A diagram of boxes for changes and arrows for causal links.
Could you photograph the change? If only the event, rewrite it.
The story beside the map: sequence, rationale, assumptions, weak spots, falsifiers.
A colleague can trace one path from activity to goal within a minute.
A ToC revised and dated as you learn.

worked_example.title: Rewrite boxes and test legibility
worked_example.setup: Rewrite two activity boxes as changes, then compare a crowded map with a clear one using the slide 74 figures.
steps: 'Hold awareness camps' becomes 'Women know and claim their entitlements'.
'Train officials' becomes 'Officials apply the new procedure'.
Crowded map: 60 boxes against a clear one of 15: 60 ÷ 15 = 4 times as many boxes.
Arrows: 100 against 20: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 times as many arrows.
worked_example.answer: The rewrites state changes you could photograph. The crowded map has four times the boxes and five times the arrows of a legible one.

mistakes: Drawing the ToC alone. The workshop is where the value is created.
Showing assumptions by implication. Notes on arrows carry them, and the narrative explains them.
Polishing the first draft. An over-polished draft signals false confidence.

recall.q: What should a box contain?
recall.a: One change, phrased as a state.

recall.q: Which way do you read the map?
recall.a: Upward, from entry-point activities to the goal.

recall.q: What does the narrative say per pathway?
recall.a: What changes in order, why each link holds, what must be true, where the evidence is weakest and what would falsify it.

recall.q: Why use cards on a wall instead of a projector?
recall.a: People move things, which builds ownership and surfaces disagreement.

recall.q: What is the legibility test?
recall.a: A colleague can trace one pathway from activity to goal in under a minute.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.big_idea: Five classic failures underlie bad ToCs, and the fifth, **confusing what you do with the change you cause**, hides the others.
in_plain_words: Activity-itis fills the map with verbs you control. Missing assumptions leave silent arrows. Leaps of logic skip the middle outcomes, and over-complexity hides muddled thinking behind a busy picture. Reverse-engineering writes the ToC after the activities to justify them.

Each has a one-look test, so a review can take ten minutes. Quieter traps include single-pathway tunnel vision, set-and-forget and having no negative pathway. Run the pre-flight checklist before showing anyone, and have someone outside the team run it too.

key_terms.meaning: Activities masquerading as outcomes.
A causal link with no stated assumption.
Intermediate outcomes skipped between two distant boxes.
A map too tangled to follow one pathway.
The route by which the programme could make things worse.

worked_example.title: Diagnose and score a map
worked_example.setup: Match four symptoms to pitfalls, then score a draft against the 7-point pre-flight checklist on slide 83.
steps: Boxes contain verbs you control: activity-itis.
Two adjacent boxes are years apart: a leap of logic.
Nobody can trace a pathway: over-complexity.
The map confirms every existing activity: reverse-engineering.
The draft passes 5 of the 7 checks: 7 − 5 = 2 fail, which is 2 ÷ 7 = 0.29, about 29 percent.
worked_example.answer: The four symptoms match the pitfalls in order, and the draft fails two of seven checks, so it needs work before it is shown.

mistakes: Keeping an activity in the middle of the map. Activities belong at the bottom as entry points.
Explaining away a complex map. If you cannot say what each arrow claims, density hides an unresolved argument.
Skipping the negative pathway. Unintended effects are usually foreseeable and unasked-about.

recall.q: What question cures activity-itis?
recall.a: 'So that what?', repeated until the answer is a change in someone else.

recall.q: What does the question 'and then what?' do?
recall.a: Converts output lists into a pathway and marks the edge of your influence.

recall.q: What is a leap of logic?
recall.a: A gap that skips the outcomes between two boxes.

recall.q: When is complexity warranted?
recall.a: When several real pathways, real feedback loops or different group routes exist.

recall.q: Name the three quieter mistakes on slide 82.
recall.a: Reverse-engineering, single-pathway tunnel vision and set-and-forget.

sections.title: Using ToC Across the Cycle
sections.big_idea: A ToC filed after the proposal wastes its value. It earns its keep across **design, MEL, adaptation and reporting**.
in_plain_words: At design the ToC stress-tests the logic before money is spent. In MEL, outcomes become indicators, assumptions become monitoring questions and pathways become evaluation hypotheses. Contribution analysis uses the ToC as its spine where no control group is possible, and its third step, ruling out other explanations, makes it an argument.

When an assumption fails, adaptive management revises the pathway and records the change on the ToC with a date and reason. In reporting, the ToC organises results around change, including broken links. Keep the map on the wall, name an owner and open each quarterly review with it.

key_terms.meaning: Revising the programme when monitoring shows an assumption failing.
A reasoned, evidenced claim that the programme helped.
Evidence that would count against the theory.
A ToC revisited, dated and owned.
A signal monitored to catch a failing assumption.

worked_example.title: Turn the map into a MEL plan
worked_example.setup: Illustrative teacher-training ToC. Derive MEL artefacts using the slide 87 table, then cost the review habit.
steps: Outcome box 'teachers use the method' becomes the indicator '% using new methods in class'.
Assumption 'teachers keep using it after supervision ends' becomes a monitoring question at endline.
Pathway 'training leads to practice leads to learning' becomes an evaluation hypothesis.
Quarterly reviews open with the ToC at about an hour each: 4 × 1 = 4 hours a year.
worked_example.answer: One indicator, one monitoring question and one hypothesis come straight from the map, and keeping it live costs about four hours a year.

mistakes: Using the ToC only at design. It then becomes a proposal annex.
Writing the MEL plan to a template. If it cannot be derived from the ToC, the plan is usually wrong.
Adapting without recording why. The record distinguishes adaptive management from drift.

recall.q: What does an assumption become in MEL?
recall.a: A monitoring question.

recall.q: Which step of contribution analysis do people skip?
recall.a: Considering alternative explanations.

recall.q: What does adaptive management do when an assumption fails?
recall.a: Adds an activity or changes the pathway, then updates the ToC with a date and reason.

recall.q: What is the hardest adaptive response to act on?
recall.a: When nothing is moving, revisit the diagnostic assumption.

recall.q: Who should own the ToC?
recall.a: A named owner appointed at inception.

sections.title: Worked Example & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: Work one full example from goal to risks, then **read one method source and one worked example**.
in_plain_words: The example is an illustrative district programme to reduce low birth weight by improving maternal nutrition. It builds a backwards pathway of five rungs, names the diagnostic assumption that nutrition is the binding constraint, and lists four links with assumptions and indicators. The social link is the weakest.

It adds an illustrative results curve, then turns each assumption into an early-warning check: stock-outs, a qualitative round, haemoglobin data and counselling contacts per worker. The further reading names the canon: Weiss, ActKnowledge and Aspen, Vogel, Comic Relief and Funnell and Rogers.

levels.label: Know what to eat, have access

diagram.caption: the pathway on slide 94, goal first

key_terms.meaning: That you found the binding constraint, here maternal nutrition.
Household food allocation, usually the weakest link.
A monitored signal tied to one assumption.
Invented for teaching; do not quote it.
Weiss 1995, ActKnowledge and Aspen, Vogel 2012, Funnell and Rogers.

worked_example.title: Size a target and pick the early warnings
worked_example.setup: Use the maternal nutrition example. Illustrative baseline: 20% low-birth-weight births, with a target of 15%. Then match breaks to checks.
steps: Change planned: 20 − 15 = 5 points.
In relative terms: 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, a quarter.
Supplement supply fails: watch stock-out reports from month one.
Household deprioritises her diet: a small qualitative round at midline.
Anaemia or infection dominates: watch haemoglobin data, if collected.
worked_example.answer: The target is a 5 point fall, a quarter of baseline. Each break point has a cheap early warning, and the diagnostic assumption deserves the first challenge.

mistakes: Quoting the example's numbers. They are invented for teaching.
Treating the pathway as controlled by the programme. Only the lowest rung is fully in its control.
Reading the whole canon. The slide suggests one methodological source and one worked example.

recall.q: What is the diagnostic assumption in the example?
recall.a: That maternal nutrition during pregnancy is the binding constraint.

recall.q: Which link is usually weakest?
recall.a: Knowledge to intake, the social link of household food allocation.

recall.q: Which link is best evidenced?
recall.a: Weight gain to birth weight.

recall.q: Name two of the four break points.
recall.a: Supplement supply fails, household deprioritises her diet, anaemia or infection dominates, frontline workers are overloaded.

recall.q: Which source is the most useful single document for a practitioner?
recall.a: Vogel's 2012 review for DFID.

notes.2: This agenda is the order in which the workbook builds a theory of change: **definition, purpose, relatives, parts, mapping method, assumptions, indicators, drawing, pitfalls, use across the cycle, then a full example**. Read sections 4 and 5 first if you are about to draw one this week. The rest explains why each step exists.
notes.4: Test every ToC on one word: **testable**. The table gives four demands, explicit, causal, testable and assumption-bearing, and shows what each becomes if it fails. Use the practical test at the bottom now: name one monitoring finding that would make you redraw the map. If you cannot, the map is decoration.
notes.5: Learn the four stages as a ladder: activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. Each arrow is a claim that **because this happened, that becomes possible**. The table makes a pointed observation: two of the four rows contain no change in anyone, and that is where most programme reporting concentrates. Real pathways also branch and stall.
notes.6: Use the symptom table as a diagnosis. **Boxes that are verbs** make a workplan, arrows with no 'because' make a results chain, and a map written after the design is a justification. The slide's tell is the absence of disagreement: a ToC nobody argued over has not surfaced the team's different theories.
notes.7: Carol Weiss's 1995 point was that complex initiatives failed evaluation because **their theories were unstated and untested**. Without a stated theory, a null result cannot say which part failed. Treat the slide as the origin of the idea: make the theory explicit first, and evaluation becomes an inquiry instead of a verdict.
notes.8: ToC moved from a way to evaluate programmes to a way to design them. The key row is the last one: **once donors made it a funding requirement**, many were produced to satisfy the requirement, which defeats testing a design. Remember this, because it explains most of the pitfalls in Section 9.
notes.9: A ToC has two faces: a diagram for structure and a narrative for reasoning. Write both. The slide's warning is that a diagram alone loses its reasoning within a staffing cycle, so **the arrows survive and the argument does not**. Keep the diagram to one page and the narrative to two to five.
notes.10: Every ToC sits in a context: place, people, politics and existing services. State the conditions your theory assumes so someone in another district can judge whether it will travel. The last row is the one teams skip: **if another organisation already supplies the missing piece**, your activity may add nothing.
notes.11: Every programme already has a theory, in someone's head. The task is to **surface it** by asking the proposal writer to draw arrows, building the map with field staff, reading the funder's strategy aloud and asking whose theory it is. These four rarely agree, and the slide says the disagreement is the value.
notes.13: Four jobs: shared understanding, better design, sharper evaluation and faster learning. The table's right-hand column is the catch: each works **only if** the team built it, it was drawn before the design was fixed, indicators come from the map and assumptions are monitored. If time is short, protect the first and the fourth.
notes.14: The chart is illustrative and unmeasured, so use it for direction: a ToC pulls effort **toward outcomes and the assumptions behind them**, while a logframe concentrates thinking lower down the chain. Ask where your own team spends its planning hours, and whether that matches the part of the chain carrying the risk.
notes.15: A plan asks what we will do and by when. A ToC asks how and why change happens. The line to remember: a plan can be **delivered perfectly and still change nothing**. Ask the last row of your own ToC: what would disprove it? A theory with no answer there is a description.
notes.16: Different people hold different unspoken theories: staff think delivery is the constraint, M&E doubts the outcome can be measured, finance doubts the budget, partners see another barrier and the community may see a different problem. A shared map surfaces these early. The slide puts the cost at **a day at design against a redesign in year two**.
notes.17: Laying out the pathway makes missing steps visible. Use the five-row table as a **checklist of links between training and learning**, and tick whether each one is in your ToC. Where a necessary link is outside your reach, you either add an activity or record it as an assumption you will monitor.
notes.18: A ToC supplies the evaluation questions: each outcome is something to measure, each arrow a hypothesis, each assumption a monitoring question and each pathway an alternative to rule out. The payoff is a better null result. Without a theory, 'it did not work' is the finding; with one, you can **say which link broke**.
notes.19: Surprises become evidence when you have a map. The four cases in the table each pair an unexpected result with a question, such as which link failed or whether another pathway operated. The slide's condition: these questions are answerable only if **the assumptions were made monitorable at design**.
notes.20: Learn the three spheres, from Outcome Mapping: control (activities and outputs), influence (outcomes you contribute to) and interest (impact shaped by many). The table gives the **claim language** for each: 'we delivered', 'we contributed to', 'this sits within'. It explains why the impact row carries no target.
notes.22: Treat the three tools as cousins. The results chain gives the spine, the logframe gives commitments and verification, and the ToC gives how and why. The advice is to use all three: **build the ToC, draw the chain out of it, then summarise it as a logframe**. Trouble starts when a team is asked for one and hands over another.
notes.23: A logframe is a four-by-four grid: four levels by four columns. It is compact, but it hides the arrows between rows. The mismatch sits in the last row of the second table: **a matrix has four assumption cells, and a map of fifteen arrows has fifteen assumptions**. Translating between them is mechanical once you see this.
notes.24: Learn the logframe's strengths and the blind spot each one carries. Compactness compresses reasoning, forced indicators reward the measurable, and the matrix is good for management but poor for learning. The sharpest contrast is the assumption column: **one per level in a logframe, one per arrow in a ToC**.
notes.25: A ToC adds branching pathways, assumptions on every arrow, a rationale, context and a narrative. The slide frames the difference as two questions: a logframe asks what will we track, and a ToC asks **why do we believe this will work**. The rationale row is most often empty and most valuable.
notes.26: The tools nest in one direction: ToC first, then results chain, then logframe, then indicators. Derive the logframe from the ToC. Going the other way is **reverse-engineering** and gives a map that justifies decisions already taken. If a logframe already exists, redraw the logic plainly and treat the contradictions as the finding.
notes.27: Use the first table to compare form, arrows, assumptions and best use, and the second to choose by reader, decision, time and complexity. The recommendation is to **build the ToC and derive the other two from it**, which costs one exercise instead of three. Independent versions disagree, and the disagreement surfaces at evaluation.
notes.28: Having a logframe does not mean having a ToC. Ask the four questions in the table of any matrix: why does this output produce this outcome, what must hold, what evidence supports the link and what else could produce the outcome. If a team cannot answer from the matrix, the slide says they have **a logframe and no theory**.
notes.29: Outcome Mapping, Outcome Harvesting, contribution analysis and process tracing pair well with a ToC when the goal runs through other actors' decisions. Read the table as a **menu by situation**: advocacy and systems change, unpredictable environments, evaluation without a control group and policy influence claims. All four take the ToC as their starting point.
notes.31: Memorise the chain: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. The third link, outputs to outcomes, **carries the most risk and the least evidence**, which is where a ToC earns its keep over a results chain. Only the first two links lie within your control. Everything above is a claim about how others will respond.
notes.32: Inputs are easy to count and tell a funder little. The slide's warning: **spending is not achievement and burn rate is not progress**, yet both get reported because they are available monthly. Use the table to hunt for uncosted inputs, especially participants' time, the largest hidden cost to the poorest.
notes.33: Outputs are countable products you control, such as 200 teachers trained. The slide warns that outputs are **necessary but never sufficient**, and that counts say nothing about usability, targeting, timing or completeness. Attach one quality indicator to each output so that 'delivered' can be told from 'delivered well enough to work'.
notes.34: The commonest ToC error is calling an output an outcome. An outcome is a change in the knowledge, attitudes, behaviour, condition or status of others. 'Teachers trained' is an output, while 'teachers teach differently' is an outcome. If your outcome sits in the **first two rows**, add behaviour change as a further link.
notes.35: Use the one-line memory: **output is what you deliver, outcome is what changes in others, impact is the long-term change**. The grammar table gives a test for each level. If the subject of the sentence is your own team, it is not an outcome however ambitious it sounds. The commonest drift is upward.
notes.36: Outcomes form a ladder from knowledge and attitude to behaviour and then condition. The third row is the warning: a **long-term outcome is regularly promised and rarely measured**, because the follow-up round has no budget once the project closes. Fund the follow-up at design, or state that it will not be observed.
notes.37: Impact is long-term, usually population-level change that many actors shape, so honest ToCs speak of **contribution** and avoid claiming sole attribution. Use the four checks to test an impact statement. Impact belongs on the map to explain why the programme exists, and the slide says it should never be a target the team is judged against.
notes.38: Do the drill before reading the answers, then apply it to your own map. Remember the test: **did you do it, or did someone else change because of what you did?** A sentence containing 'and' holds two results. The slide says teams usually reclassify a quarter of their boxes, almost always downward.
notes.40: Backwards mapping starts from the long-term goal and asks what must be true just before it. The direction is the whole method. Starting from activities guarantees the map will find your activities sufficient. The slide's payoff is **an uncomfortable finding**: the goal needs four preconditions and the programme can act on two.
notes.41: Use the five questions at each backward step: what must be true just before, why would that produce it, what evidence says so, who has to act and can we influence it. Recording the **actor at each step** is the underused move. When most actors are other people, the design needs partnerships and influence strategies.
notes.42: A precondition is an outcome that must exist before a higher outcome becomes possible. Read bottom to top, the stack becomes a causal pathway. The test table checks four things: is it required, is it a change, is it at the right distance and can it be observed. If you cannot say **how you would know it had been met**, it is vague or two preconditions.
notes.43: The picture shows a backwards-mapped pathway: the goal at the top, the preconditions beneath it and the activity at the base, with arrows showing causal direction. Read it **upward as a claim** and downward as the design logic. Check that every box describes a change and only the base describes an action.
notes.44: Real pathways branch and converge. Map each pathway separately and then show where they meet. Convergence usually means that the pathways are all **required**, so say which. The slide's blunt conclusion: if you can fund only one required pathway, the honest theory says the programme alone will not reach the goal.
notes.45: Keep mapping back until you reach outcomes your programme can act on, which are your entry points. The table gives three honest reasons to stop and three dishonest ones. The dishonest ones are a long diagram, an uncomfortable next step and unwillingness to name something. If the necessary entry point is out of reach, **partner, advocate or redefine the goal**.
notes.46: Ask two questions at every step. Necessary: if you drop one precondition, does the chain break? Sufficient: if all are true, does the next box follow? The slide says necessity is easy and **sufficiency is where theories break**. A no on sufficiency means a missing box or an assumption, depending on whether you can act on it.
notes.47: Follow the five facilitation steps: agree the goal, ask what must change just before, repeat downwards, identify entry points and surface assumptions. Use cards on a wall. **Protect step five**, because it is the one that gets cut when a workshop overruns and it is what makes the map testable.
notes.49: Every arrow hides an assumption, a belief about why one outcome leads to the next. If an assumption fails, **the link breaks however well you deliver**. The middle row of the table deserves attention: links that feel obvious are the ones evaluations most often find broken. Audit every arrow at the end of drafting and write the because.
notes.50: Learn the four kinds: causal-link, rationale or evidence, external condition and diagnostic. Each is tested differently, from monitoring the two connected outcomes to reading the literature to tracking an external indicator. The diagnostic type is the most consequential, because it asks whether you have identified the **binding constraint** correctly.
notes.51: A rationale is evidence, theory or experience that a link tends to hold. Grade it with the table: systematic review or trial evidence, prior evaluation, practitioner and community experience, then 'it seems reasonable'. The slide says community knowledge is evidence, and **'it is obvious' carries no weight** as a rationale. Name the source.
notes.52: Use the sentence form to surface assumptions: **IF teachers are trained, THEN practice improves, BECAUSE they apply what they learn**. The slide says the BECAUSE is the assumption and the thing most likely to fail, and adds a condition about class size, materials and supervision. Write one for every arrow.
notes.53: An assumptions column and a risk register hold the same information for two audiences. Plot each assumption by likelihood of failing and consequence. The chart is illustrative; the top-right corner marks **load-bearing assumptions** to design around and monitor first. If a load-bearing assumption is likely to fail, the theory says the programme will not work.
notes.54: Hunt for the killer assumption deliberately: the one that, if it fails, collapses the theory. The slide's example is households letting women keep their earnings. It is often **social or political and rarely technical**. Put an early check into the monitoring plan with a date, so the answer arrives while the design can still change.
notes.55: You cannot remove external conditions, but you must name them and monitor the ones most likely to move. The table pairs each with a source to watch. The slide's last row is the most controllable: **partner commitments should have named deliverables and dates**, with no room for general goodwill.
notes.56: Treat each assumption as a hypothesis and write down what you would observe if it were false. The cheap tests in the table take a day of fieldwork or twenty conversations. The most valuable and least done is the last: **ask non-users why**, because it tells you which assumption is wrong.
notes.58: Every outcome needs an answer to 'how will we know this happened?', and the answer is an indicator. The first row of the table is the whole test: a good indicator **moves only if the outcome is real**. An outcome indicator that rises when you deliver the output is measuring the output under another name.
notes.59: SMART is a checklist you can bend. The slide's deeper test is whether the indicator faithfully reflects the outcome under it, because SMART will pass a precisely measured proxy for something adjacent. Add the question SMART omits: **what would this indicator read if the programme failed entirely?**
notes.60: Match indicator to level: counts for outputs, change in others for outcomes, condition for impact. The common mistake is hanging only output indicators on outcome rows. The slide notes the cost rises down the column, so decide at design **which rows you will fund**, and say so instead of listing unfunded outcome indicators.
notes.61: Use numbers to detect change and stories to understand it. The table pairs each question with a method. The last two rows, why it did not change for some and what else happened, are reached only by qualitative work. Collect qualitative material **before you know the quantitative result**, or the stories merely illustrate it.
notes.62: An indicator needs a baseline, a target and, later, an endline. The table lists what goes missing without each. The slide's two rules: set a date and an owner for every baseline at inception, and **set targets after the baseline lands**, since a target chosen blind is a number with no commitment.
notes.63: For each indicator, name the means of verification: the data source and method. The table compares sources by strength and weakness. The under-discussed hazard is **courtesy bias**: people report more benefit to the organisation that gave them something. Use independent enumerators at least at endline for the outcome claim that matters most.
notes.64: Choose a few indicators that move decisions. Ask of each candidate what decision it would change and who will look at it. If the answer is nobody, **do not collect it**. The slide treats respondent goodwill as a depletable resource, since communities surveyed repeatedly for numbers nobody uses stop answering carefully.
notes.65: Read the table top to bottom as the change moving up the pathway: delivery, usable quality, ability, practice and difference made. The second row matters: a post-test separates **'we ran a training'** from 'people can do the thing'. If your indicator set jumps from row one to row four, a null result is uninterpretable.
notes.67: Boxes hold outcomes phrased as changes, arrows show causal direction, branches show parallel pathways and notes on arrows carry assumptions. The drafting rule is to **keep same-level boxes at the same height**, so missing steps appear as gaps in a row. Number your boxes so the narrative can refer to the link from one to another.
notes.68: The worked map shows two pathways, attendance and effective teaching, converging on one goal, with an assumption written at the join. A converging arrow is ambiguous between 'and' and 'or'. Convergence usually means both are necessary, so **say which reading applies in words** on the map.
notes.69: Write outcomes as changes and test each box: **could you photograph the change?** If you can only photograph the event, rewrite it. The slide's pairs, such as 'conduct hygiene sessions' becoming 'families practise safe hygiene', each raise a measurement question and demand an assumption on the arrow beneath.
notes.70: Write the story beside the map. For each pathway the narrative should say what changes in order, why each link should hold, what must be true, where the evidence is weakest and what would falsify it. The slide says the fourth item, the weak spots, **makes a narrative credible**. Keep it to a few pages.
notes.71: A ToC drawn with the team, partners and community is a shared belief, and one drawn alone is a document. Use the facilitation choices in the table: start from the goal, use cards on a wall, separate groups then merge, and write assumptions as you go. **Photograph the wall** before anyone tidies it.
notes.72: Ask whose theory this is. Communities hold knowledge about what drives change in their lives that no logframe captures. The slide's last question is rarely asked: **who benefits from things staying as they are?** Where someone gains from the status quo, a capacity-building pathway will not shift it.
notes.73: Treat the first draft as a draft. The slide says an over-polished first version signals false confidence, and the table lists when to revise: a baseline lands, an assumption fails, an unexpected outcome appears or the context shifts. **Date every version** and note what changed and why.
notes.74: Keep the map legible: main pathways only, detail in the narrative, indicators in a table and assumptions numbered. Use the one-minute test: can a colleague trace one path from activity to goal in under a minute? Sixty boxes and a hundred arrows are, in the slide's words, **muddled thinking rendered at high resolution**.
notes.76: Use the pitfall map as a ten-minute review before discussing content. Five failures: activity-itis, missing assumptions, leaps of logic, over-complexity and reverse-engineering. The slide says the fifth underlies the others and is the **hardest to see from inside**, because a reverse-engineered map is internally consistent.
notes.77: Activity-itis fills the map with things the programme will do. The cure is mechanical: for every activity box ask **'so that what?'** until the answer is a change in someone else, then keep the change and demote the activity. Activities still belong at the bottom, as entry points.
notes.78: The 'so that' clause is where the outcome hides. Use the table to turn outputs such as '500 women trained' into outcomes by asking 'and then what do they do?'. Asked three times, this converts most output lists into a pathway, and **the point where you can no longer answer marks your sphere of influence**.
notes.79: A silent arrow is a claim nobody has examined. The slide's example is 'women earn income, so women are empowered', which hides the assumption that she controls how the income is spent. These four are **well-documented broken links**, and all four look self-evident as arrows. Audit every arrow and write the because.
notes.80: A leap of logic skips the outcomes in between. The slide's example runs from training health workers to falling child deaths with three missing boxes. Each missing box is also a **missing measurement point**: a programme that maps only the two ends can report activity and mortality and nothing that explains either.
notes.81: Over-complexity is the opposite failure: a map so dense nobody can follow one pathway. The slide says complexity is no proof of rigour and often hides unresolved thinking. Test it by asking what each arrow claims. If a map must be complex, **split it**: one overview plus a detailed map per pathway.
notes.82: Three quieter mistakes, plus a fourth in the table: reverse-engineering, single-pathway tunnel vision, set-and-forget and no negative pathway. Each turns a living theory into a dead document. Add the fourth to your own practice: **draw the pathway by which the programme could make things worse** and put a monitoring check on it.
notes.83: Use this checklist before showing the map to anyone: does every box describe a change, is there a clear path, does every arrow carry an assumption, are the load-bearing and external assumptions named, is there a rationale, is it simple enough to explain in two minutes, did **the people it serves help shape it**? Then have an outsider run it.
notes.85: A ToC filed after the proposal wastes most of its value. Its real life runs across design, MEL, adaptation and reporting, and the last three cost nothing extra if the map stays current. The cheapest habit is to **open each quarterly review with the ToC**: which links moved, which assumptions held.
notes.86: At design the ToC stress-tests the programme before money is spent, which the slide calls the cheapest failure you will ever have. Use the four questions in the table. The third is where a ToC most often changes a design: **a load-bearing assumption becomes an activity**, and the programme gets stronger.
notes.87: In MEL the ToC turns into a measurement plan: outcomes become indicators, assumptions become monitoring questions and pathways become evaluation hypotheses. The slide's warning: if the plan cannot be derived from the ToC, **usually the plan is wrong**, because it was written to a template. Record context conditions so a positive result can be transferred responsibly.
notes.88: Contribution analysis uses the ToC as its spine where a controlled experiment is impossible. Follow the five steps in the table. The step people skip is the third: **ruling out other explanations** turns a narrative into an argument. The verdict is whether it is reasonable to conclude the programme made a difference.
notes.89: Adaptive management means that when monitoring shows an assumption failing, you change the programme and record it on the ToC. The table pairs each signal with a response. The last row is the hardest and most important: **if nothing on the pathway moves, the problem may differ from the one the programme was built for**.
notes.90: A ToC lets you report **change**: here is the change we contributed to, here is the evidence, and here is where the theory did and did not hold. The slide says reporting a broken link makes a stronger document than reporting only success. Ask first whether your funder's systems reward candour.
notes.91: Keep it living: revisit at every major review, date each version, pin the current map where the team can see it and use it to onboard staff. None is expensive. The slide's diagnosis is that ToCs end in drawers because **nobody owns keeping them current**. Name the owner at inception.
notes.93: The worked example is a district programme to reduce low birth weight through maternal nutrition. The figures are illustrative. Study the third row of the table, the diagnostic assumption: **maternal nutrition is the binding constraint**. If anaemia, infection or short birth intervals dominate, the logic will be sound and the effect small.
notes.94: Read the pathway from the bottom: counselling, supplements and ANC linkage, then knowledge and access, then better eating, then weight gain, then fewer low-birth-weight babies. The control column shows how quickly the pathway **leaves the programme's control**: two links up, it depends on households and supply systems.
notes.95: Work through the four links and their indicators. The load-bearing assumption is the second: knowing is useless if the household cannot afford or reach the food. The slide calls the **social link** usually the weakest, which points to involving the household as well as the mother.
notes.96: The chart is illustrative and uses invented numbers. Its shape is the lesson: **a baseline, a credible trajectory and a dated target**. Use it to check your own indicators for the same three features, and recall that targets should be set after the baseline lands.
notes.97: Every bullet is an assumption from the table turned into a monitoring question. The right-hand column lists an early warning for each: stock-out reports, a small qualitative round, haemoglobin data and counselling contacts per worker. The slide's advice: **write the early-warning column next to the assumption column**.
notes.98: The reading list gives the canon: Weiss for the founding essay, ActKnowledge and Aspen for the backwards-mapping method, Vogel for a candid review of practice, Comic Relief for grantee guidance and Funnell and Rogers for programme theory. Read **one methodological source and one worked example**.
notes.99: The five takeaways are your revision list, each with a one-minute test you can apply to any ToC. The slide says most maps fail at least one test. If you take only one, **take the fourth**: every arrow should carry a because, since the assumptions are where the theory can break.
